 Trump administration drops legal fight to overhaul student loan forgiveness program
 The reversal leaves the program’s existing eligibility rules in place after two courts ruled the Education Department overstepped its authority.
 Jasmine Andersson Thu, October 22, 2026 at 12:32 PM UTC 3 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. The U.S. Department of Justice initially appealed the decision. (Anna Moneymaker via Getty Images) The Justice Department has dropped its appeals of two court rulings blocking eligibility restrictions for a popular student loan forgiveness program for public-sector workers.
 The government had filed notices of appeal Aug. 27, taking the Massachusetts case to the First Circuit Court of Appeals and the D.C. case to the D.C. Circuit.   
 Court documents released Wednesday show both appeals have now been dropped, with each side paying its own fees, AP reported.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The appeals challenged two decisions made in June that struck down the Trump administration's bid to restrict the Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) program, which cancels the debt of public-sector workers and nonprofit employees after 10 years of qualifying service. 
 The administration had sought to exclude certain organizations from the program based on activities it considered unlawful, including some related to immigration and gender-affirming care.
 Dan Zibel, an attorney for the group Student Defense, said in a written statement, called the decision "a significant victory for millions of Americans who have dedicated their careers to public service."
 What is the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program?
 The program, established under President George W. Bush in 2007, forgives remaining federal student debt for people who have worked in public service jobs for 10 years and made 120 qualifying monthly payments.
 Advertisement Advertisement To date, the program has written off student loans for more than 1 million eligible Americans, including nonprofit workers, teachers, social workers, nurses and other public workers.
 However, few borrowers received forgiveness in the program's early years, and the program drew criticism over high rejection rates. By the time President Joe Biden took office in 2021, only about 7,000 borrowers had received forgiveness, according to The Boston Globe . Biden's administration introduced a temporary waiver that year to ease some of the barriers.
 What was the administration trying to change?
 President Donald Trump signed an executive order in March 2025, "Restoring Public Service Loan Forgiveness," directing the Education Department to exclude organizations engaged in activities the administration considered illegal.
 The department then finalized a rule in October 2025 that would have given the education secretary, currently Linda McMahon, power to disqualify nonprofit employers from PSLF if she determined they had a "substantial illegal purpose."
 Advertisement Advertisement The rule's definition of "substantial illegal purpose" covered certain immigration-related activities, gender-affirming care, support for terrorism, alleged illegal discrimination, reproductive care for minors and protest-related conduct. It also included conduct such as "aiding or abetting" federal immigration law violations and a pattern of aiding and abetting illegal discrimination.
 Lawsuits challenging the decision were filed within days of its publication by cities and counties, as well as states and nonprofits. The plaintiffs included 22 states and D.C., nonprofit employers, unions and cities.
 On June 30, 2026, one day before the rule was due to take effect, federal judges in Massachusetts and Washington, D.C., struck it down in separate cases. Massachusetts ruled that the restriction exceeded the Education Department's authority and violated the First Amendment by tying eligibility to an organization's speech or viewpoint.
 In D.C., a judge ruled that the rule exceeded the department's authority under the Higher Education Act. 
 Advertisement Advertisement Because both courts vacated the rule rather than only pausing it, the previous eligibility rules from the program have stayed in effect.
